genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the future bargewoman grew up beside a waterway
as a child she watched the boatmen make their craft fast to the quay
she began her working life as a hand on a sand barge
she learned to read the movement of the current
her training covered approach manoeuvres and slowing down
she learned to lay a heavy hull along the edge despite the wind
after long seasons she was given charge of a convoy
that convoy could tow two further craft
she now teaches her trade to beginners
she tells them to think ahead to the next manoeuvre
text: The woman who would one day steer barges spent her childhood in a cluster of houses beside a narrow waterway. From the towpath she watched the boatmen make their craft fast to the quay, then slip away at first light towards the next lock. Her working life began with a hand's job aboard a barge loaded with sand, and it was there that she learned to read what the current was doing. The training that followed was hard. She had to master the approach, to slow without grazing the bank, to lay a heavy hull along the edge while the wind pushed against her. Long seasons later she was given a convoy of her own, one that could tow two further craft behind it. She teaches beginners now, and the rule she repeats to them is plain: think of the manoeuvre after this one, because water forgives nothing done in haste.

units: a funicular now serves a very steep slope
a winding road used to provide that link
the climb now asks less effort of travellers
the shops at the top of the rise take more custom
use of the line runs past what the operators predicted
the cars are packed at busy times
the wait at the foot of the slope puts off some passengers
removing the road shuttles leaves isolated households without a service
the works are judged sound technically but wrongly sized
text: The funicular on the hillside deserves a mixed verdict. Its cars climb a slope so steep that only a winding road used to link the two levels, and the swap has cut both ways. Since the climb now costs a traveller nothing at all, the small shops at the top of the rise have won back custom they had given up on, and their takings have climbed sharply week after week. Yet use of the line has run so far past what the operators predicted that the cars leave packed all afternoon, and the queue building at the foot of the slope turns away a share of would-be passengers, who give up and walk off instead. One further effect is still argued over: the road shuttles have gone, and with them the only service reaching the most isolated households. So the works convince as a piece of engineering, and disappoint as a matter of capacity.

units: the writer of the message has moved far from where he works
his coach journey took a very long time
traffic jams made his arrival time impossible to predict
he arrived worn out before he had even begun
someone at work suggested a combined solution to him
he now reaches the station with a folding bike
he finishes the journey on a regional train
the bike lets him get past the heavy traffic
he saves half a period on his old journey
he invites the person he is writing to come and try the route
text: You asked me whether moving out had made a mess of everything. At the start, yes. The coach took forever, crawling behind a line of cars that never shifted, and I never had the faintest idea what time I would land. I turned up worn out before I had even begun. Then someone at work suggested what I ought to have thought of myself: break the trip in two. So now I set off with a folding bike, thread my way past the stalled traffic down to the lower station, and finish on a regional train, where I sit down at last with the bike tucked under the seat. It has saved me half a period on the old run, and I arrive cheerful rather than fuming. Rain is the one snag, though a cape sorts that out. Come over one quiet morning, take the spare bike, and try the route with me. You will see.

units: a specialist in urban planning answers a reporter's questions
she compares the tram with the bus on a reserved lane
the tram carries more passengers at every run
rails demand costly and lengthy works
the bus can be put into service far more quickly
the bus copes badly with heavy crowds
the tram keeps its lead on the busiest corridors
she warns against deciding without studying local demand
she judges the route to matter more than the type of vehicle
text: Lay rails, or paint a reserved lane? We put the question to a specialist in the planning of large towns. Her answer is blunt: the two options never come out equal, and the setting settles the matter. A tram, she explains, takes on far more passengers at every run and keeps moving while the general traffic stalls; against that, it demands a heavy, expensive worksite that shuts streets for whole seasons together. A bus on a protected lane starts running very quickly and can be shifted elsewhere if demand moves, yet it struggles the moment the crowds thicken, and on the busiest corridors the tram holds its lead. She refuses any clean verdict. Study what the demand actually is before you pick the hardware, she says, because a badly drawn route will ruin whatever runs along it.

units: a passenger questions a sailor on the deck of a night ferry
the sailor lists what he loves about his work
he mentions the smell of wet rope
he speaks of the noise of the chains being worked
he brings up the brightness of the beacons on dark water
he values the hush of sleeping travellers
he says he knows the regulars by their walk
he states that the crossing home never resembles the crossing out
text: On the deck of the night ferry a passenger asked the sailor what still held him to the work. He laid a hand on the rail and answered with a list, as though he had had it ready for years. He loved the smell of wet rope, he said, that thick scent which soaks into the palms and stays there. He loved the clatter of the chains being hauled before they came alongside, a din that tells you the shore is near. He loved the beacons burning on black water, counted off one by one all the way to the mouth of the channel. He loved the hush of travellers dozing against their bags under blankets rough enough to scratch. He knew the regulars by their walk alone, that careful, hesitant step on wet plating. And before he went back up to the bridge he added that the crossing home had never once resembled the crossing out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first heavy loads were shifted on wooden rollers
the spoked wheel took weight out of vehicles
a harness bearing on the shoulders replaced the strap that pressed on the animals' throats
that change increased the pulling power available
metalled tracks stopped the wheels sinking
wooden rails then guided the wagons in the mines
steam did away with dependence on animal strength
every advance bore on the contact between vehicle and ground
text: Before any machine existed, shifting a heavy mass meant heaving it onto wooden rollers and carrying each one round to the front again as it came free. The spoked wheel came later and took weight out of the body of the cart, so that less effort was needed to set it moving from a standstill. Then the harness changed, and that mattered more than anything else: the strap that pressed on the animals' throats gave way to a collar bearing on the shoulders, and teams could suddenly pull loads that had been out of reach. Tracks were metalled so that rims stopped sinking into the mud, and wooden rails were laid in the mine galleries to guide the wagons. Steam closed the sequence by doing away with muscle altogether. Every step attacked the same weak point, which is where the vehicle meets the ground.

units: a slowdown can appear with no obstacle and no crash
one driver brakes lightly for a trivial reason
the vehicle behind brakes harder out of caution
the amplification travels back along the queue
the queue ends up at a complete standstill
the wave of slowing moves back while the cars move forward
keeping enough space ahead softens the effect
sitting too close makes the spread worse
text: A line of cars will sometimes come to a halt although nothing blocks the road ahead and no crash has occurred anywhere on it. The mechanism behind this can be described exactly. One driver eases off for some trivial reason: a clumsy entry, a moment of inattention, a slight rise in the road. The driver behind sees the brake lights and presses a little harder, out of caution. The third driver reacts more sharply still, and the gap between them tightens. Step by step the amplification travels back up the column until vehicles a long way behind the first one must stop dead. What is odd is that this wave of slowing moves backwards while the cars themselves keep going forwards. The remedy fits into one instruction: keep a comfortable gap in front of you, and never sit on the tail of the driver ahead.

units: a coach of walkers takes a mountain track
a rockfall blocks the way above a ravine
the width of the passage rules out turning round
the driver refuses to reverse back down several bends
the passengers shift the lighter stones
a farm tractor arrives from the hamlet nearby
the tractor drags the main block aside with a chain
the journey resumes with a moderate delay
the woman driving the tractor refuses any payment
text: The coach carrying the walkers had taken a stony track that wound its way up towards the pass. Round a bend hanging over a ravine, fallen rock lay right across the way. There was no width there to turn a coach in, and the driver flatly refused to reverse down a run of bends as rough as those. The passengers climbed out and began shifting the lighter stones by hand, but the largest of them would not budge whatever they tried. A farmer from the hamlet just below turned up at last on her tractor, looped a chain round the boulder and hauled it onto the verge in three unhurried pulls. The coach set off again only moderately late, to applause from the whole group of walkers. Asked what she wanted for the job, she only shrugged, swung the tractor round and drove back down towards her cattle sheds.

units: the text explains how to choose between a night train and a long-distance coach
it advises comparing the fares of the two options first
the night train saves paying for a room
the coach calls at stops the railway ignores
the reader must check the arrival time before booking
booking a berth well away from the corridor is recommended
a soft bag is needed since there is no storage space
the coach imposes halts that break up sleep
the final choice depends on how much rest matters
text: Torn between the night train and the long-distance coach? Work through it in stages. Compare the fares of the two first, but add to the ticket price what a room would have cost you, because that is usually where the train claws back the difference. Then look at the list of stops, since the coach calls at small towns the railway passes nowhere near. Check what time you arrive before you book anything, or you will be put down before the ticket office opens. If you go by train, pick a berth well away from the corridor and bring a soft bag, or you will sleep against your luggage with your knees folded up. If you go by road, accept in advance the compulsory halts that will wake you in the small hours. Then settle it with one question: do you want to arrive rested, or to pay as little as you can?

units: a report describes the reopening of an abandoned railway line
crews have replaced the rotten sleepers
a tunnel overrun by roots has been cleared
a footbridge has been added for cyclists
people living beside the line dread the noise of night trains
local growers mean to send their goods out by rail
passengers will try the line before it opens formally
the fares have not yet been settled
text: Rusted rails that the undergrowth had been quietly swallowing for a generation are taking trains again. Several things stand out from our visit to the works now reopening the line. The track, first: the crews have pulled out the rotten sleepers and cleared a tunnel where roots had reached down as far as the ballast itself. Access, next: a steel footbridge now spans the cutting, so that cyclists need no longer scramble down the embankment to reach the far side. Worries, too: people living beside the line dread the rumble of trains at night and are already asking for acoustic screens. Hopes, last: the growers of the surrounding countryside intend to send their harvests out by rail. Passengers will ride the length of the line before it opens formally; the fare table, meanwhile, has yet to be settled.
